clue.text: Permit cry of pain in rage?  No time

indicators.note: 'No' tells you the following item is absent, so it is removed from the word it sits in
one item placed in another means the first sits inside the second

blocks.note: temper is an outburst of anger
T is the standard abbreviation for time
the exclamation you make when hurt

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether letting out a howl of pain in a fit of fury is allowed, and is told there is no time.
explanation.walkthrough: The time is removed first, and only then does the cry go inside what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To empower someone is to give them authority or leave to act, so it is a synonym of the verb permit.

clue.text: Broadcast is copied in serial form

indicators.note: to broadcast is literally to scatter widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A programme on air is a repeat of something shown as a series.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' reads as the subject of the sentence, a TV show, but it is the instruction to rearrange the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Episodic describes something told in instalments or episodes, which is exactly what a serial is.

clue.text: Sweet old man not moving east

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man
still means motionless
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A dear elderly gentleman who refuses to head east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet old man' reads as one description of a person, but 'Sweet' is the definition and 'old man' is father.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is a small chewable lozenge or confection, one kind of sweet (British for a piece of candy).

clue.text: One can, entertained by joker, miss point in play

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken in by them, so one item is held within the other

blocks.note: a wag is a joker or wit
the Roman numeral for one
a tin is a can
to forgo is to go without or pass up
a dot is a point

explanation.surface: Someone holding a can, kept amused by a comedian, fails to see the point of a stage drama.
explanation.walkthrough: Beckett's absurdist play is famous for audiences missing its point, so the surface doubles as a comment on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Waiting for Godot is Samuel Beckett's celebrated two-act stage drama, so it is an example of a play.

clue.text: Lamented bird appearing on front of tabloid in colour

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter only
items placed in another word sit inside it

blocks.note: red is a colour
an egret is a white heron
the opening letter of tabloid

explanation.surface: A sorrowful bird turns up on a newspaper front page in colour print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamented bird' reads as one phrase, a mourned creature, but 'Lamented' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamented and regretted are both past tenses of verbs for feeling sorrow about something.

clue.text: Base linked to era producing amount of film

blocks.note: the foot of something is its base
an age is an era

explanation.surface: A military base tied to a historical period yields some film reels.
explanation.definitionFit: Footage is recorded film material, originally measured by its length in feet.

clue.text: Place for discussion in university in fashion

indicators.note: something in another thing is enclosed by it

blocks.note: to fashion is to form or shape
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A trendy venue on campus for debate.
explanation.walkthrough: U sits inside FORM. 'Fashion' looks like style, but here it is the verb to shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a meeting place or medium where ideas are debated, from the Roman public square.

clue.text: Conducted groups high above small seats for audience

blocks.note: orchestras are ensembles led by a conductor
tall means high
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Guided tour parties sit up high over the little chairs where spectators sit.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'above' just puts one piece before the next. In British theatres the stalls are the ground-floor seats.
explanation.definitionFit: The orchestra stalls are the front rows of theatre seating nearest the pit, where spectators sit.

clue.text: Takes on commercial work, climbing street

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: a commercial is an advert
op is short for opus, a work
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to do an advertising job while walking uphill along a road.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt an idea or responsibility is to take it on as one's own.

clue.text: Officer among aliens ignored

indicators.note: among means within the group, so the answer lies inside the following words

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: An officer is snubbed by visitors from another planet.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a junior commissioned officer in the navy, so it is a kind of officer.

clue.text: Delivery from popular vocalist carrying weight

indicators.note: one who carries a thing holds it, so the other item goes inside

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
a singer is a vocalist
W is the abbreviation for weight

explanation.surface: A parcel arrives from a well-loved, rather heavy pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an inswinger is a ball that curves in towards the batsman; 'Delivery' pretends to be a parcel.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a delivery is a single ball bowled, and an inswinger is one type of such ball.

clue.text: Get over being annoyed

blocks.note: first meaning: to go across, as a road or river
second meaning: irritated or angry

explanation.surface: Advice to stop being irritated and move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get over' looks like 'recover from', but it is the literal sense of passing to the other side.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb meaning to traverse something and an adjective meaning angry or irritated.

clue.text: Opening achieved by one in working for diamonds

indicators.note: one item placed in another sits inside it
working suggests letters set in motion and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A gap in the market is created by someone labouring to find gems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working for' reads as employment, but 'for' is fodder: put I in FOR, rearrange to ORIF, then add ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: An orifice is a hole or aperture, especially a mouth or vent, so it is a kind of opening.

clue.text: Reach junction going west in Welsh town

indicators.note: in an across entry, westward means right to left, against the normal reading direction

blocks.note: to get somewhere is to reach it
a seam is a line where two pieces join

explanation.surface: A traveller arrives at a road junction heading west in a town in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Maesteg is a former mining town in Bridgend county, South Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Maesteg is a town in the Llynfi valley of South Wales, so it is an instance of a Welsh town.

clue.text: Not allowed to be hostile for example with hint, dropping name

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so that item leaves the word

blocks.note: ill as in ill will, unfriendly
e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
to intimate is to hint
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Being unfriendly, for instance by dropping hints and forgetting someone's name, is forbidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hostile' gives the short word as in ill will; 'dropping name' applies only to the hint.
explanation.definitionFit: Something illegitimate is unlawful or unauthorised, outside what the rules permit.

clue.text: Notes Roman made all over the place

indicators.note: something all over the place is scattered and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Messages written by an ancient Roman were scattered everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin plural suits the Roman in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda, the Latin plural of memorandum, are written reminders or brief messages, which are notes.

clue.text: Important person is being excited, accepting Oscar

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so another letter is added among these
excited letters are stirred up into a new order

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A celebrity gets thrilled when receiving an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oscar looks like the film award, but it stands for one letter added to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Big noise is informal slang for an influential or prominent figure, a bigwig.

clue.text: Upset head of state trapped by upper-class weed

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
something trapped is held inside another thing

blocks.note: U is the label for upper-class usage
the nettle is a stinging weed
the opening letter of state

explanation.surface: A head of state, upset, finds themselves caught in a patch of posh weeds.
explanation.walkthrough: S goes into NETTLE after its N, behind U. U for upper-class comes from the 1950s U and non-U debate on British posh usage.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsettle someone is to disturb or agitate them, a synonym of the verb upset.

clue.text: Caught by evil demon, state criticism

indicators.note: evil suggests something corrupted or twisted, so the letters are distorted

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
letters to be rearranged
a nation is a state

explanation.surface: A country, seized by a wicked fiend, faces censure.
explanation.definitionFit: Condemnation is strong public disapproval, a severe form of criticism.

clue.text: Bad result hurt

blocks.note: food that is off has gone bad
an end is an outcome or result

explanation.surface: A poor outcome caused pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hurt' reads as past tense, but it is the present-tense verb, matching offend.
explanation.definitionFit: To offend someone is to wound their feelings, so it means to hurt them.

clue.text: Delight about answer let out

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: to revel is to take great delight
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys giving away the solution.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal a secret is to disclose it, which is what letting it out means.

clue.text: Rowing boat stuck behind loud river transport

blocks.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
R is the abbreviation for river
an eight is a racing boat with eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: A racing shell gets stuck behind a noisy barge on the waterway.
explanation.definitionFit: Freight is goods carried by vehicle or ship, and as a verb means to transport cargo.

clue.text: I had to support favourite, taken up without enthusiasm

indicators.note: in a down entry, taking something up means reading it from bottom to top

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone had to back the favourite in a race, though without much enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, to support is to sit below, so ID comes under the reversed favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Tepid means lukewarm, and figuratively a tepid response is one lacking keenness or warmth.

clue.text: Followers showing energy come together and run around

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy
to unite is to come together
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Supporters are full of vigour as they gather and jog around.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants or aides accompanying an important person, so they are followers.

clue.text: Correct people engaged by editor

indicators.note: those engaged by an employer are taken in by them, so one item is held inside another

blocks.note: ED is the abbreviation for editor
men are people

explanation.surface: The staff hired by a newspaper editor are right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct' reads as an adjective, but it is the verb meaning to fix text, as an editor would.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to make corrections to a text, so it is a synonym of the verb correct.

clue.text: Silent pal bothered one involved in radio quiz?

indicators.note: bothered means upset or troubled, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A quiet friend gets flustered when appearing as a contestant on a broadcast quiz show.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: panellists also appear on TV shows and committees.
explanation.definitionFit: A panellist is a member of a panel of guests on a broadcast quiz or discussion programme.

clue.text: Swindled, receiving instrument reduced in strength

indicators.note: something receiving another item takes it in, so that item goes inside

blocks.note: to do someone is slang for cheating them
a lute is a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: Someone cheated, taking delivery of a watered-down violin.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'do' someone is British slang for cheating them, so swindled gives the past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Diluted describes a liquid weakened by adding water, so it has been made less strong.

clue.text: Serious about following novelist endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means without its end, so the final letter is cut off
following sends the word for about to come after the shortened writer, not before

blocks.note: Jane Austen, the English novelist
re means concerning or about

explanation.surface: A sober remark about trailing after a writer who never stops.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Austen is the novelist; 'endlessly' trims only her name, not the whole wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere means stern and severe in manner, so a grave, serious person can be called austere.
